2027-03-29.title: First Monday of Resurrection
2027-03-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-29.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The first week of the Resurrection, traditionally the week of the newly baptised (neophytes): each day of this week shares the joy of Easter.
2027-03-29.verse: In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.
theo: The first week after Easter was, in the ancient Church, the week of the newly baptised. Those who had come up from the font on the night of the Resurrection, dressed in white, came to the church every day to hear what had happened to them. The readings of this week still speak to them, and to every baptised Christian who wants to understand Easter from the inside. Isaiah speaks to a city that had been hated and abandoned: “Whereas you have been forsaken and hated, with no one passing through, I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age.” Then comes a promise that no city of stone could ever fulfil: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you by night; but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory. Your sun shall no more go down, or your moon withdraw itself; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.” The days of mourning ended on Easter morning. The Book of Revelation sees the same city at the end of time, needing no sun or moon, “for the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). The neophytes carried lit candles from the font; every Christian carries that light into an ordinary Monday.

On the day of Pentecost Peter stands up in Jerusalem and preaches the first Christian sermon. He reasons from the Psalms: David said that God would not abandon his Holy One to Hades or let him see corruption. But David died; “his tomb is with us to this day.” So David was speaking as a prophet, of the Messiah. “This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses. Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear.” The empty tomb of Jesus stands beside the full tomb of David: the difference between them is the whole Gospel. Peter speaks to his own people, the house of Israel, with the love of a brother, calling them to recognise their Messiah; the Church reads his words as a call to every one of us. Paul then shows how this new life is received: not by our works but by faith. “For what does the scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.’” And he quotes David's joy: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the one against whom the Lord will not reckon sin.” The newly baptised had just experienced exactly this: every sin washed away, not because they had earned it, but because they believed and were baptised into the Risen Christ. Faith is not opposed to good works; it is the root from which they grow. But the root comes first, and it is a gift.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, but every word looks towards Easter. “I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you. In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.” The Resurrection is not only a fact about Jesus; it is the source of our life: because he lives, we live. He promises that the Father and he will come and make their home in whoever loves him and keeps his word: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.” He promises the Advocate: “But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.” And he leaves his own gift: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.” This is the first word the Risen Lord will say when he comes through the locked doors on Easter evening: Peace be with you. The peace of Easter is not the absence of trouble but the presence of the Risen One. In the Syro-Malabar Qurbana, the priest gives the peace to the people before the anaphora, and the people pass it to one another: the peace of the Risen Lord, carried from the altar into our homes. In this first week of Easter, a family can make a simple practice of it: each evening, before sleep, say to one another, ‘The peace of the Lord be with you’.
conn: “The LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19); the heavenly city has no need of sun or moon, “for the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).
David's tomb and the empty tomb.
Peter quotes Psalm 16:10, “you do not give me up to Sheol, or let your faithful one see the Pit”; Paul makes the same argument at Antioch (Acts 13:35–37).
“And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6); Jesus “was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).
Paul quotes Psalm 32:1–2. On Easter evening the Risen Lord gives the apostles the power to forgive sins (John 20:22–23).
“Father of orphans and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5); Jesus promises, “I will not leave you orphaned” (John 14:18).
Jesus promises his peace (John 14:27) and gives it on Easter evening: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the promise of John 14 is kept: the Father and the Son come and make their home in those who receive the Body of Christ with love. Because he lives in us, we live.
The kiss of peace before the anaphora is the gift of the Risen Lord: not the peace the world gives, but his own, passed hand to hand from the altar.

live: Each evening this week, say to each other: The peace of the Lord be with you.
Make a good confession in this Easter week and thank God for the sins he no longer reckons.
Before reading the Bible each day, say: Come, Holy Spirit, teach me and remind me.
Pray this week for those baptised at Easter, and for your own godchildren.
fathers: He said, because I live, you also will live. He lives because he is God and because he has risen; we will live because he lives. His life is the cause of ours. He did not say ‘you live’, but ‘you will live’, because our resurrection is still to come in the body, yet already begun in faith and hope.

To the newly enlightened: you were led by the hand to the holy pool of divine Baptism, as Christ was carried from the Cross to the tomb. You went down into the water three times and came up again, and so in a figure you imitated the three days' burial of Christ. In the same moment you died and were born, and that saving water became both your tomb and your mother.
magis: The grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, cleansing us from our sins; justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ and is conferred in Baptism.
Our justification comes from the grace of God; grace is the free and undeserved help God gives us to respond to his call.
Jesus promises the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who will teach and remind the disciples of all he said.
The ultimate end of the whole divine economy is the entry of creatures into the perfect unity of the Trinity; even now we are called to be a dwelling for the Holy Trinity.
The newly baptised are dressed in white and given a lighted candle: Christ has enlightened them, and they are to walk as children of the light.
saints: 29 March–3 April: first week of the Resurrection. Friday 2 April: in the East Syriac tradition, the feast of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar).
2027-03-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and living, you promised not to leave us orphans, and you have come to us. Because you live, we live. Make your home in us with the Father, send us the Advocate to teach us and remind us of your words, and give us your peace, which the world cannot give. Keep the newly baptised in the light of their Baptism, and let us all walk as children of the light. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

quick: Isaiah: the LORD will be your everlasting light; your days of mourning are ended.
Peter: David's tomb is with us; this Jesus God raised up, and we are witnesses.
Jesus: I will not leave you orphaned; because I live, you also will live.
2027-03-29.action: This evening, say to each one at home: The peace of the Lord be with you.
2027-03-29.question: Do I live as one who has been forgiven and made a dwelling of God?
kidsaint: Peter once denied Jesus three times because he was afraid. But after Jesus rose, Peter stood up in Jerusalem and told thousands of people: “This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.” Lesson: Jesus can turn a frightened heart into a brave one!
2027-03-29.special: First Monday of Resurrection. Easter week, the week of the newly baptised.
term: From the Greek for ‘newly planted’: a person newly baptised. In the early Church the neophytes wore white garments all through Easter week and came daily to church to learn the meaning of the sacraments they had received.

family.explain: Before Jesus died, he told his friends: “I will not leave you alone. I am coming back to you.” And he did! He rose from the dead. He also said: “Because I live, you will live too.” And he gave them a special gift: his peace. That means a quiet, safe feeling in our hearts because Jesus is with us.
family.intention: We pray for children who feel alone or afraid, that they may know Jesus is with them.
family.ask: Ask: “When do you feel worried? Let us give that worry to Jesus and ask for his peace.”

illus: A retired schoolteacher in Kottayam, a widow for ten years, used to say that she was never really alone in her house. Her neighbours thought it was the talk of an old woman. One day a young mother asked her how she could live so peacefully by herself. She pointed to the small crucifix and the Bible on her table. “When my husband died,” she said, “I read the words, ‘I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you.’ I decided to believe them. He has kept his promise every day.” The young mother began to visit her every Monday. She said later that she came to comfort the old teacher, and always went home comforted herself.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you promised not to leave us orphans. Come among us now and give us your peace. Amen. Alleluia!
share: The LORD will be your everlasting light (Isaiah 60:19). What mourning in my life does Easter end?
This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses (Acts 2:32). How am I a witness to the Resurrection?
Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven (Romans 4:7). Do I live as one who has been forgiven?
Because I live, you also will live (John 14:19). Where do I need the life of the Risen One today?
interc: For the newly baptised, that they may persevere in the grace of their Baptism.
For orphans and those who feel abandoned, that they may know the love of the Father.
For the Jewish people, that God may bless them in his faithfulness, and for friendship between Christians and Jews.
For all who are troubled and afraid, that the peace of Christ may fill their hearts.
For our families, that the Father and the Son may make their home with us.
pm.close: Father, you raised your Son from the dead and gave him the promise of the Holy Spirit. Pour out that Spirit on us, make your home in us, and keep us in the peace of Christ. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, in the early Church this week belonged to the newly baptised. They came to church every day in their white garments to understand the new life they had received. Today the readings speak to them, and to all of us who were baptised.

Isaiah promised a city that had been abandoned: “The LORD will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.” On Easter morning the days of mourning ended. Christ is our light that never sets.

Peter preached: David died and his tomb is still with us; but “this Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.” The empty tomb beside the full tomb: that is the whole difference. Jesus is alive, and he has poured out the Holy Spirit.

Paul tells us how we receive this life: by faith, like Abraham, who “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” And he sings with David: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven.” Our sins were washed away in Baptism, not because we earned it, but as a gift.

Jesus promised: “I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you… because I live, you also will live.” He promised that the Father and he would make their home in us, and that the Holy Spirit would teach us. And he gave us his peace, not as the world gives.
This week, let us carry his peace home. Each evening, say to one another: The peace of the Lord be with you. Because he lives, we live. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus promised his friends: ‘I will not leave you alone.’ And he kept his promise: he rose from the dead, and he is always with us!
Jesus gives us his peace, a quiet, happy feeling inside. Tonight, say to your family: ‘The peace of Jesus be with you!’

concl: The Risen Christ is our everlasting light, our righteousness and our peace.
Because he lives, we live: let us live like it this week.
